analysis.one_liner: Lets adults buy hearing aids for mild-to-moderate hearing loss over the counter, without a prescription.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress ended, though its language became law the following year.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill directed the FDA to create a new category of over-the-counter hearing aids for adults with mild to moderate hearing loss, with safety and labeling rules, and let them be sold in stores, by mail, or online without seeing a licensed professional first. It also stopped states from adding their own different requirements. The bill was introduced jointly by a Democrat and a Republican in December 2016 but was referred to a Senate committee and never taken up before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults with mild to moderate hearing loss who cannot afford prescription hearing aids, which typically cost thousands of dollars and require visits to a licensed dispenser. The bill would have let them buy devices directly, in person, by mail, or online, at whatever price a competitive market produces.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to create an over-the-counter hearing aid category that adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing impairment can buy without the involvement of a licensed person, through in-person, mail, or online sales.
Directs the FDA to write regulations ensuring safety and effectiveness, including consumer labeling, with proposed rules due within three years of enactment and final rules 180 days later.
Bars state and local governments from imposing requirements on over-the-counter hearing aids that differ from the FDA rules, preventing states from recreating the prescription barrier.

analysis.who_pays: Companies and licensed professionals who earn money from the current prescription model: hearing aid manufacturers that sell through controlled dispenser channels, and audiologists and hearing aid dispensers who charge for fitting and follow-up visits. Consumers would bear the usual risk of self-treating without a professional evaluation of whether their hearing loss has a medical cause.

drawbacks.text: The bill would let people self-diagnose: a device bought online without a licensed evaluation could miss a medically treatable cause of hearing loss, which is the standard safety objection raised by hearing professionals.

Over-the-counter devices were limited to adults with mild to moderate hearing loss, so people with severe loss or children would still need the professional channel, and the FDA had three years to write the rules, delaying any price relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit was large: hearing aids routinely cost thousands of dollars per device largely because a prescription-and-fitting requirement limits competition, and roughly tens of millions of Americans have hearing loss but most do not use hearing aids. The main cost is the safety trade-off of self-diagnosis, which the bill addressed with FDA labeling and efficacy rules rather than eliminating oversight. The design was narrow and reasonable, though the three-year rulemaking window meant benefits would arrive slowly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate on December 1, 2016, sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and sat there until that Congress ended three weeks later without any action.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill for herself and Senator Charles Grassley, making it bipartisan from the start.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on December 1, 2016.
No committee action, vote, or floor action followed; the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and licensed dispensers who profit from the prescription hearing aid model were better off, since the bill died and their protected market stayed intact. Consumers gained nothing from this Congress, although the same proposal was introduced again in the next Congress and became law in 2017, so the idea survived the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Over-the-Counter Hearing Aid Act of 2016 in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Charles Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN) in the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and cosponsored by the senior Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee, so it was not a partisan fight; it simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would have opened the prescription-only market to direct-to-consumer sales, eroding the distribution model that keeps hearing aid prices high. It also created a potential new product category for manufacturers willing to compete in it.
Their state-protected role as the required gateway to a hearing aid would have ended for adults with mild to moderate loss, removing the fitting and evaluation fees that are part of every purchase.

industries.industry: Consumer electronics and direct-to-consumer device makers
industries.note: A legal over-the-counter category would have let new entrants sell affordable hearing devices online and in stores to ordinary consumers.
